video_title: Higher Rates Could Burst the AI Bubble — Here’s What to Own Instead
gist: Jesse Felder (The Felder Report) tells Maggie Lake the Fed has begun a longer-than-expected hiking cycle amid a hot, stagflationary economy, which he expects to burst an AI bubble already showing credit stress (Oracle, SoftBank/OpenAI) and overbuild. He favors value stocks, energy and broad commodities in a supply-driven super cycle, and sees gold pressured until a Fed pivot or a bond-market intervention.

themes.theme: New Fed hiking cycle and inflation dynamics

insights.claim: Jesse Felder believes the Fed has started a genuine new rate-hiking cycle that will last longer than investors appreciate, because it has missed its inflation target since March 2021 while unemployment is low.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Markets that swung from pricing cuts to hikes may still be underpricing the length of the hiking cycle.
insights.quote: the rationale for tightening [clears throat] has has rarely been so clear-cut as it is today

insights.claim: Nominal GDP growth in Q2 was so strong that only six quarters since 1990 matched it, the prior instances being 2005 (before the housing bust) and 1999 (before the dot-com bust).
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Historically this pace of nominal growth has marked late-cycle peaks just before major bubbles burst.

insights.claim: Felder argues the US is running the economy hotter than at any point in roughly 35 years while financial conditions are as loose as they have ever been.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Hot economy plus loose conditions strengthens the case for further Fed tightening.

insights.claim: Inflation pressures are building across the board: record-high diesel prices, import prices rising at the fastest pace in decades (partly AI-driven), producer prices ripping higher, manufacturing surveys citing pricing pressure, and food prices turning up.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Broad-based pipeline inflation argues against a quick end to hikes.

insights.claim: A new El Nino could produce a real spike in food prices next year, adding to inflation risk.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Agricultural commodities and food inflation could become another upside inflation shock.

insights.claim: Historically the 10-year Treasury yield rises at least 100bp on average during a Fed hiking cycle (50bp low end, 200bp+ high end); starting from about 5%, Felder sees 6% as the average outcome and 6.5-7% as plausible.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Implies meaningful further downside in long-duration bonds and higher mortgage/consumer borrowing costs.

insights.claim: Felder applies an Occam's razor view to rising long-term yields: an oversupply of Treasury debt colliding with an oversupply of corporate debt issued to fund the AI boom, with supply outpacing demand.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: AI-related debt issuance is a direct driver of higher long-end yields, linking the AI boom to bond pricing.

insights.claim: The consumer discretionary sector is the worst-performing sector this year, signaling consumers are already struggling before further rate hikes.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Further hikes would hit an already-weak consumer; defensives like staples and healthcare are starting to show life.

insights.claim: Felder describes the current setup as very stagflationary: raising rates into an already stressed consumer and housing market while the economy depends on the AI bubble.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Stagflation is historically bad for both stocks and bonds simultaneously.

themes.theme: Bond market fragility: basis trade and private credit

insights.claim: The New York Fed has reportedly been talking to major banks about the highly leveraged Treasury cash-futures basis trade, which comes under pressure when rates and bond volatility rise, raising the risk of a Treasury market accident.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: The move from 5% to 6% on the 10-year may not be smooth; a disorderly unwind could force Fed intervention.
insights.quote: it might not be just a a smooth ride from five to six. It could be we could, you know, see a an accident in in the Treasury market

insights.claim: Felder cites Fitch saying private credit defaults are already about 6.5%, and PIMCO saying that including payment-in-kind loans, defaults are nearly 20% of loan portfolios.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Rising rates add stress to an asset class where hidden distress may already be large.

insights.claim: Private equity funds are stuck with zombie companies they cannot offload, but Felder views private credit as the bigger problem.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Exposure to private markets carries rising liquidity and default risk in a hiking cycle.

themes.theme: AI bubble: funding stress and end-of-cycle signals

insights.claim: Felder argues that rising interest rates are historically the trigger that bursts speculative bubbles, and the AI bubble is now facing them.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: The combination of a hiking cycle and a stretched AI trade raises the odds of a violent repricing.
insights.quote: There's really nothing like rising interest rates to burst a speculative bubble.

insights.claim: Citing Roger McNamee, Felder says AI labs made a huge bet on AGI that has not worked, open-source models are eating their lunch, and markets are increasingly unwilling to give them more money.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Funding fatigue for frontier labs threatens the capex chain that supports AI equities.

insights.claim: Credit markets are tightening on AI: distress in Oracle loans and bond prices, distress in loans tied to a Jane Street data center build, and SoftBank seeking to borrow at a junk rating to fund OpenAI.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Credit spreads on AI-linked issuers are an early warning that the money may be running out for the AI trade.

insights.claim: Felder claims semiconductor earnings forecasts are 100% dependent on data center buildouts that physically cannot be built fast enough, so the slowdown is already happening and earnings estimates will not be met.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Consensus semiconductor earnings estimates may be structurally too high.

insights.claim: Felder says OpenAI's attempted IPO effectively failed because banks told it demand was not there for a trillion-dollar-plus listing of a company projecting about $300 billion in losses, and that 'safety' was used as a cover story for the delay.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: A failed mega-IPO would signal the limit of public-market appetite to fund AI losses.

insights.claim: Felder accuses Anthropic of claiming profitability using 'bogus' adjusted accounting that excludes expenses, likening it to WeWork's adjusted EBITDA.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Non-GAAP profitability claims by AI labs warrant skepticism ahead of any IPO.
insights.quote: they are claiming to be profitable based on on literally bogus accounting

insights.claim: Felder concludes the AI cycle is near its end because the amount of capital needed to fund the next phase is becoming too large for markets to supply.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Investors heavily exposed to AI infrastructure face end-of-cycle risk.

insights.claim: Felder expects no effective federal put behind AI: Scott Bessent has said the best regulation is to make AI firms liable rather than indemnify them, and there is bipartisan anti-data-center and anti-big-tech sentiment from figures like Steve Bannon, Bernie Sanders, Lina Khan and David Sacks.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Political backing for AI may be weaker than assumed; legal liability is a growing risk.

insights.claim: Citing Matt Levine, Felder argues investors should weigh AI labs' 'negative TAM' (potential legal liability), likening it to tobacco companies whose TAM and lawsuit exposure scaled together, against claims like a $30 trillion TAM equal to US GDP.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Liability tail risk is unpriced in AI valuations.
insights.quote: what's your negative TAM right what is your negative TAM that's what investors have to start thinking about

themes.theme: AI overbuild, efficiency gains and the dark-fiber analogy

insights.claim: Every investment boom ends in overinvestment, and as AI moves from undersupply to oversupply, extreme pricing (e.g., in memory) pushes companies to become far more efficient with memory and compute, as with dark fiber after the dot-com boom.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Efficiency gains compound overbuild, implying a deeper bust for AI infrastructure suppliers.

insights.claim: Memory suppliers worldwide are investing billions to add capacity, and China is subsidizing its chip industry for security reasons, creating a massive supply response that Felder sees as end-of-cycle.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: A large supply response is the classic signal of a capital cycle peak, the opposite of commodities today.

insights.claim: Small language models run locally with the right harness and agents can deliver results comparable to data-center frontier models on a laptop, reducing demand for centralized compute.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Edge/local inference threatens the data center demand thesis.

insights.claim: Enterprises are reportedly shifting away from OpenAI and Anthropic models toward cheaper open-source models run on local servers, both for cost and to avoid IP being harvested by the labs.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Pricing power and revenue growth of frontier labs may disappoint.

insights.claim: Felder argues the best long-term outcome for AI would be a huge bust that drives compute costs to near zero, just as the dot-com bust enabled Google and Facebook, laying groundwork for sustainable business models.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: The durable AI winners may emerge after the bust, not among today's infrastructure leaders.
insights.quote: the best thing for the technology longer term would be a huge bust

themes.theme: Concentration risk and rotation to value and real assets

insights.claim: Per Bloomberg, AI infrastructure stocks make up 40% of the S&P 500, three chip stocks are 28% of emerging market indexes, half of investment-grade bond issuance this year is AI-tied, and 90% of VC funding is AI.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Diversification across stocks, EM and credit offers little protection from an AI unwind.

insights.claim: In rising-rate environments value stocks historically beat growth because higher discount rates hit long-duration earnings harder; the only exception was 1999-2000, after which value soared as the dot-com bubble burst.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Tilting toward value and old-economy names is the playbook if rates keep rising.

insights.claim: During high inflation, financial assets (stocks and bonds) do poorly while real assets do phenomenally well, typically at each other's expense.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Supports reallocating from financial assets into commodities and precious metals.

insights.claim: Energy is about 3% of the S&P 500 and Nvidia is worth more than the entire energy sector; Felder thinks energy could rise to 10% of the index and institutional gold allocations could go from about 0.12% (as stated) to 5%.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Massive under-ownership leaves room for multi-year flows into energy and gold.
insights.quote: Nvidia is worth more than the entire energy sector

insights.claim: The energy sector is up 50%-plus this year yet investors still show no interest and keep chasing big tech.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Lack of investor participation despite strong performance suggests the trade is early.

themes.theme: Commodity super cycle driven by supply and capital cycle

insights.claim: Felder says the commodity super cycle is far from over because super cycles are driven by the capital cycle, and producers are not yet investing massively in new oil, gas or copper supply; that investment would mark the beginning of the end.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Watch producer capex announcements as the key signal for the top of the commodity cycle.

insights.claim: Commodity demand is less elastic than assumed: energy demand barely fell in the financial crisis and only collapsed under pandemic lockdowns, so supply, constrained by 15 years of near-zero investment, is what matters.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: A recession may dent but not break the commodity bull case.

insights.claim: At about $100 a barrel, oil is arguably undervalued: oil-to-S&P 500 and oil-to-gold ratios are near record lows and the inflation-adjusted price is near its 40-year average; a problematic spike needs well over $120-150.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Upside risk in oil remains despite the headline price.
insights.quote: at $100 a barrel, oil, you could argue, is still undervalued

insights.claim: A lesson from 1973-74 is that stocks reacted most to the downside after the oil crisis ended, as markets realized prices would not fall back because of long-term supply problems.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: The end of an immediate supply crisis may not be the all-clear for equities.

insights.claim: With a 5% 10-year and 7-8% corporate borrowing costs, producers lack incentive to fund new wells and mines; Felder thinks a commodity spike-induced recession that lowers borrowing costs while prices stay high could finally trigger the supply response.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: High cost of capital extends the supply shortage and the commodity cycle.

themes.theme: Gold: leads commodities, awaits a Fed pivot

insights.claim: Felder's framework is that gold leads and the rest of commodities follow; gold topped around January-February this year and the broader commodity complex, especially oil, is now catching up.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Favor broader commodities and oil over gold in the near term.
insights.quote: gold leads and the rest of the commodities market follows

insights.claim: Felder expects gold to stay under pressure as markets accept a sustained hiking cycle rather than one or two hikes.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: Near-term gold weakness may persist while rates rise.

insights.claim: Gold should bottom ahead of the next dovish Fed pivot, possibly after 150-200bp of hikes; Fed intervention in the bond market during an inflationary episode, e.g. due to a basis-trade blowup, would be among the most bullish catalysts for gold.
insights.speaker: Jesse Felder
insights.so_what: A forced Fed bond-market rescue is the key trigger to add gold aggressively.
insights.quote: That would be one of the most bullish kind of catalysts I think for the gold prices.
